subject: Copywriting
subcategory: The Science of Storytelling in Ads
title: The Villain in Ad Stories
description: Learn The Villain in Ad Stories in one minute.

hook.text: Apple's 1984 ad cast IBM as Big Brother. Every great ad story needs a villain—something the hero fights against.

buildup.text: The villain gives the story stakes. Without an enemy, there's no tension. Without tension, there's no engagement.

discovery.text: The villain doesn't have to be a competitor. It can be a problem: acne, debt, bad Wi-Fi, or wasted time.

twist.text: The strongest villain is the status quo. 'Things don't have to be this way' is the most compelling battle cry.

climax.text: Dollar Shave Club made overpriced razors the villain. Warby Parker made expensive glasses the villain. Problem as enemy.

punchline.text: Every story needs a villain. Make the problem the enemy.

quiz.question: What is often the most compelling villain in ad stories?

details.summary: Every compelling ad story needs a villain — the obstacle, frustration, or enemy that the hero must overcome. In advertising, the villain might be a competing approach, a status quo, an industry norm, or the problem itself. A clear villain gives the story stakes and makes the hero's victory...
details.whyItMatters: Without a villain, there's no conflict, and without conflict, there's no story. Defining the villain clarifies the brand's purpose and gives the audience something to root against, amplifying their desire for the product that defeats it.
takeaways: The villain creates conflict that makes the story compelling
Villains can be tangible competitors, abstract problems, or systemic frustrations
The villain should be something the audience already dislikes or fears

faq.question: Should the villain be a competing brand?
faq.answer: Rarely by name — it can seem petty and invite legal issues. Instead, villainize the approach or mindset the competitor represents. Apple's '1984' villainized conformity (IBM's approach), not IBM directly. The audience connected the dots without the ad making an explicit attack.

faq.question: Can the villain be too scary?
faq.answer: Yes. If the villain feels insurmountable, the audience loses hope and disengages. The villain should be formidable enough to create real stakes but defeatable with the right tool (your product). Fear that the hero can overcome is motivating; fear that feels hopeless is paralyzing.
